title: Types of Machine Learning
abstract:
Machine learning splits into four families, and the split is made on exactly one
question: how much supervision does the algorithm receive? This document
works through all four — supervised (regression and classification),
unsupervised (clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection,
association rule mining), semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning — with
the data layout each one expects, the mathematical objective each one optimises,
worked examples, runnable code, and the decision rule for identifying which
family a new business problem belongs to.

blocks.t: The Organising Question
The single axis of classification

Machine learning types are decided by the amount of supervision the
algorithm needs in order to get trained. "Supervision" means: does the
dataset contain the right answers?

blocks.cap:
The four families. Note the asymmetry — supervised learning has two
 children decided by the data type of the target, while unsupervised has
 four children decided by what kind of structure you are hunting for.

blocks.t: Vocabulary: the output column has many names

The column you are trying to predict is called, interchangeably: the
target, the label, the dependent variable, the
response, or simply $y$. The columns you predict from are the
features, inputs, independent variables,
predictors, or $X$. Interviewers switch between these freely.
Supervised Learning
The one-sentence version

You show the model the input columns together with the right output
column, and it learns the pattern that maps one to the other.
The data layout

Every row carries its answer. The learner's job is to find a function
$f$ such that $f(\text{IQ},\text{CGPA})\approx\text{Placement}$, and — this is
the part that matters — such that it keeps working on a student it has
never seen.
Formal statement

Given $D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ with $x_i\in\mathbb{R}^d$ drawn i.i.d. from an
unknown $P(X,Y)$, find $\hat f$ minimising the expected risk
R(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim P}\big[L(f(x),y)\big].

$P$ is unknown, so in practice we minimise the empirical risk
$\widehat R(f)=\frac1n\sum_i L(f(x_i),y_i)$ and control the gap
$R(f)-\widehat R(f)$ with regularisation, validation and more data. That gap is
exactly what "overfitting" names.
The two sub-types
The split is made purely on the data type of the target column.

blocks.cap:
Same inputs, different targets. Left: the target is continuous, so we
 fit a line and measure error in the target's own units. Right: the target is a
 label, so we fit a boundary and count mistakes.

head: Regression
Classification
rows: Yes / No, Spam / Ham, Dog / Cat / Rabbit
A best-fit line, plane, or curve
Linear/Polynomial regression, SVR, regression trees, XGBoost
Logistic regression, SVM, decision trees, random forest, Naive Bayes, KNN

blocks.t: The trap: a numeric-looking target that is not regression

A target encoded as $0/1/2$ for Low / Medium / High looks numerical but is
categorical. If you run regression on it, the model will happily predict
$1.37$ and will assume the distance from Low to Medium equals Medium to High.
Ask what the numbers mean, not what dtype pandas assigned. Conversely,
predicting a house's price band (₹$0$–$50$L, $50$L–$1$Cr, $\ldots$)
is classification even though the underlying quantity is continuous.

blocks.t: Unsupervised Learning
The one-sentence version

You show the model only the input data — there is no answer column at
all — and it finds the structure itself.

Because there is no $y$, "prediction" is not even a well-posed request. There
is nothing to predict — you do not know what the answer would be. So the
questions change shape entirely.

blocks.cap:
The four unsupervised tasks. Each answers a different question about
 the same unlabelled table.

blocks.t: Clustering — "which rows belong together?"

Groups similar data points into clusters. On our student data, a clustering
algorithm might discover three natural groups:
Clustering manufactures a label that did not exist

Notice what just happened: you started with no output column and created
one. Cluster IDs can now be fed into a supervised model, used to segment
customers for marketing, or used to route new users. This is the most common
industrial use of clustering: e-commerce customer segmentation.

With $n$-dimensional input, clusters live in an $n$-dimensional hyperspace that
you cannot see. The algorithm still finds them; you simply cannot plot them
without first reducing the dimensions — which is the next task.
Algorithms: K-Means, Hierarchical/Agglomerative, DBSCAN, Gaussian Mixture Models.
Dimensionality reduction — "which columns are redundant?"
Reduces many features to fewer meaningful ones. Two distinct motivations:

items:
Performance. With 1000 input columns the algorithm runs slowly
 and, past a point, the extra columns stop improving the result — they only add
 noise and sparsity (this is the curse of dimensionality, Topic 32).

Visualisation. You cannot plot 50 dimensions. Compress to 2 or 3
 and the same relationships become visible to the eye.

blocks.t: Why compression does not have to destroy information

Suppose two of your columns are number of rooms and number of
bathrooms. These are strongly related — houses with more rooms have more
bathrooms. A dimensionality-reduction algorithm can replace both with a single
new column, roughly "square footage", losing almost nothing. It found the
direction along which the data actually varies.
Algorithms: PCA, LDA (supervised variant), t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders.
Anomaly detection — "which row does not belong?"
Finds data points that look very different from the rest.

head: Domain
The anomaly you are hunting
rows: A defective unit on the line
A loan application with a falsified profile
An aircraft engine whose (heat generated, vibration intensity) pair sits far from every engine ever measured
A server whose latency profile suddenly leaves the normal envelope

blocks.t:
The aviation example is the cleanest mental model: plot every engine as a point
in (heat, vibration) space. Nearly all points form a dense blob. A new engine
landing inside the blob is fine. A new engine landing far outside is flagged —
without anyone ever labelling an engine as faulty.
This is why anomaly detection is usually unsupervised

Anomalies are rare and often novel. If you had thousands of labelled examples of
every failure mode you would use classification. You typically do not — which
is exactly why you must learn "normal" and flag departures from it.
Association rule mining — "what occurs together?"
Finds items or events that co-occur.
People who buy bread often buy butter.
People who watch this film often watch that one.
The formal machinery is three numbers. For a rule $A\Rightarrow B$:
Support, confidence, lift

$$\text{support}(A\Rightarrow B) &= P(A\cap B) && \text{how often the pair appears at all}\\ \text{confidence}(A\Rightarrow B) &= P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)} && \text{given }A\text{, how often }B\\ \text{lift}(A\Rightarrow B) &= \frac{P(B\mid A)}{P(B)}=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)P(B)} && \text{how much }A\text{ raises }B$$

Lift is the one that matters. $\text{lift}=1$ means $A$ and $B$ are independent
and the "rule" is an illusion. $\text{lift}>1$ means genuine positive
association. High confidence with lift $\approx 1$ is the classic false discovery:
everybody buys milk, so "buys anything $\Rightarrow$ buys milk" has high
confidence and tells you nothing.
Algorithms: Apriori, ECLAT, FP-Growth.
Semi-Supervised Learning
The one-sentence version

Partly supervised, partly unsupervised. A small amount of data is
labelled by humans; a large amount is unlabelled. The model uses both.

The motivation is economic. Labels are expensive — a radiologist annotating
scans, a lawyer tagging contracts — while raw data is nearly free.

head: 10{,}000 emails
rows: labelled by humans as spam / not-spam \hfill $\rightarrow$ supervised part
no labels at all \hfill $\rightarrow$ unsupervised part

blocks.t:
The model learns the pattern from the 500 labelled emails, then applies that
pattern across the 9{,}500 unlabelled ones — using the structure of the
unlabelled mass to sharpen a boundary that 500 points alone could never place
confidently.

blocks.cap:
Why the unlabelled data helps. With 8 labels alone the boundary is
 badly under-determined. The unlabelled points reveal that the data forms two
 dense blobs; the boundary belongs in the sparse region between them.

blocks.t: The assumption that makes it work

Semi-supervised learning is not free. It relies on the cluster
assumption: points in the same dense region tend to share a label, and the true
decision boundary passes through low-density regions. When that assumption
fails, unlabelled data can actively hurt — you will confidently
propagate a wrong label across an entire cluster.

Google Photos is the everyday example: it clusters all your photos by face
(unsupervised), then asks you to name one person once (supervision), and
labels the whole cluster.

Techniques: self-training / pseudo-labelling, label propagation,
co-training, consistency regularisation.
Reinforcement Learning
The one-sentence version

The model learns by trial and error, receiving rewards or
penalties for its actions.

blocks.cap:
There is no dataset here. An agent acts, the environment responds with
 a new state and a scalar reward, and the loop repeats millions of times.

blocks.t: The self-driving car, in RL vocabulary

head: RL term
Symbol
In the car
rows: $+1$ for staying in lane, reaching destination

blocks.t: The objective

The agent seeks a policy $\pi$ maximising expected discounted cumulative
reward:

The discount factor $\gamma$ encodes patience. $\gamma\to0$ makes the agent
greedy for immediate reward; $\gamma\to1$ makes it willing to accept a small
loss now for a large gain later — which is precisely what braking before a
corner requires.
What makes RL structurally different

In supervised learning you are told the right answer for each input. In RL you
are only told how good the outcome was, possibly thousands of steps after
the decision that caused it. Two problems follow, and they are the whole
difficulty of the field:

items: Credit assignment — which of the last 500 actions earned the crash?

Exploration vs. exploitation — do you repeat the route you know is
 decent, or try an unknown one that might be better?

blocks.t:
Algorithms: Q-Learning, SARSA, DQN, Policy Gradients, PPO, Actor-Critic.
Uses: game playing (AlphaGo), robotics, ad bidding, RLHF for language models.

blocks.t: Code: All Four Families

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. SUPERVISED -- REGRESSION   (X and a NUMERIC y)
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
X = rng.uniform(5, 10, (200, 1))                 # CGPA
y = 1.9 * X.ravel() - 6 + rng.normal(0, 1, 200)  # package in LPA
reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print("predicted package for CGPA 8.5:", reg.predict([[8.5]]))

# =====================================================================
# 2. SUPERVISED -- CLASSIFICATION  (X and a CATEGORICAL y)
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 2))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)          # placed / not placed
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
print("class:", clf.predict([[0.4, 0.9]]),
      "probability:", clf.predict_proba([[0.4, 0.9]]))

# =====================================================================
# 3. UNSUPERVISED -- CLUSTERING   (X only; we INVENT the label)
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
X = np.vstack([rng.normal((3, 3), .8, (60, 2)),
               rng.normal((8, 7), .8, (60, 2)),
               rng.normal((4, 8), .8, (60, 2))])
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("cluster ids:", km.labels_[:10])           # <-- a label that did not exist
print("centroids:\n", km.cluster_centers_)

# =====================================================================
# 4. UNSUPERVISED -- DIMENSIONALITY REDUCTION
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 10))                  # 10 columns
X[:, 5:] = X[:, :5] @ rng.normal(0, 1, (5, 5))   # last 5 are redundant
p = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X)
print("variance kept by 2 components:", p.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

# =====================================================================
# 5. UNSUPERVISED -- ANOMALY DETECTION
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (200, 2))
X = np.vstack([X, [[6, 6], [-7, 5]]])            # two planted anomalies
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=0).fit(X)
print("flagged as anomalies:", np.where(iso.predict(X) == -1)[0])

# =====================================================================
# 6. SEMI-SUPERVISED  (only 8 of 200 rows carry a label)
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.semi_supervised import LabelSpreading
X = np.vstack([rng.normal((3, 3), 1, (100, 2)),
               rng.normal((8, 8), 1, (100, 2))])
y = np.full(200, -1)                             # -1 means "unlabelled"
y[[0, 1, 2, 3]]         = 0                      # 4 labels for class 0
y[[100, 101, 102, 103]] = 1                      # 4 labels for class 1
ls = LabelSpreading(kernel="knn", n_neighbors=7).fit(X, y)
print("labels inferred for all 200 rows:",
      np.bincount(ls.transduction_))

# =====================================================================
# 7. REINFORCEMENT LEARNING  (tabular Q-learning, no dataset at all)
# =====================================================================
n_states, n_actions = 6, 2
Q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
alpha, gamma, eps = 0.1, 0.9, 0.2

def step(s, a):                       # a toy "environment"
    s2 = min(max(s + (1 if a == 1 else -1), 0), n_states - 1)
    r  = 10 if s2 == n_states - 1 else -1        # reward only at the goal
    return s2, r

for episode in range(2000):
    s = 0
    for t in range(50):
        a = rng.integers(n_actions) if rng.random() < eps else int(np.argmax(Q[s]))
        s2, r = step(s, a)
        # Bellman update: bootstrap off the best value of the next state
        Q[s, a] += alpha * (r + gamma * Q[s2].max() - Q[s, a])
        s = s2
        if s == n_states - 1:
            break
print("learned policy (best action per state):", Q.argmax(axis=1))
How to Identify the Family of a New Problem
Summary
Everything on one page

items: The taxonomy is decided by how much supervision the algorithm gets.

Supervised $=$ input $+$ correct output. Splits by target dtype:
 numerical $\to$ regression, categorical $\to$ classification.

Unsupervised $=$ input only. Four jobs: clustering
 (group rows), dimensionality reduction (compress columns),
 anomaly detection (find outliers), association rules
 (find co-occurrence).

Semi-supervised $=$ a few labels $+$ a lot of unlabelled data.
 Works only under the cluster assumption. Solves the labelling-cost problem.

Reinforcement $=$ no dataset; an agent acts in an environment and
 learns from delayed scalar reward. Hard because of credit assignment and
 the exploration/exploitation tradeoff.
Clustering is the bridge: it manufactures a label column where none existed.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked

Q. Predicting house price bands (cheap / mid / premium) — regression or
classification?

Classification. The target is categorical even though the underlying quantity is
continuous. If they wanted the number, it would be regression.
Q. You have 1 million images and budget to label 2{,}000. What do you do?

Semi-supervised. Label the 2{,}000 (ideally chosen by active learning —
the points the model is least certain about), then use pseudo-labelling or label
propagation over the rest. State the cluster assumption you are relying on.
Q. Is anomaly detection supervised or unsupervised?

It can be either, but is usually framed as unsupervised because anomalies are
rare and often novel — you cannot enumerate the failure modes in advance. If
you do have plentiful labelled anomalies, treat it as imbalanced classification.
Q. Why can't you just use clustering when you have labels?

You can, but you would be discarding information. Clustering optimises for
geometric compactness, not for separating your classes; the clusters it
finds may cut across the labels you care about. Labels are expensive — use them.
Q. Give an example where reinforcement learning is the only option.

Any problem where the correct action is unknown but the outcome is scorable:
game playing, robot locomotion, real-time ad bidding. Nobody can write down the
right Go move for a given board, but you can score the final win/loss.
Q. A rule has 90% confidence but lift of 1.0. Is it useful?

No. Lift $=1$ means the consequent is no more likely given the antecedent than
it is in general. The confidence is high only because the consequent is common
(e.g. almost every basket contains milk).
